content: Nasopharyngeal angiofibroma, also known as juvenile nasopharyngeal angiofibroma (JNA), is a histologically benign but locally aggressive vascular tumor that arises in the posterior nasal cavity. It predominantly affects adolescent males. Patients typically present with unilateral nasal obstruction and recurrent episodes of epistaxis (nosebleeds). The tumor is classified into three stages based on the Radkowski Classification System: Stage I: Limited to the nasal cavity and/or nasopharynx (Ia) or with extension into one or more paranasal sinuses (Ib). Stage II: Minimal extension through the sphenopalatine foramen into the pterygomaxillary fossa (IIa), filling the pterygomaxillary fossa with anterior bowing of the posterior wall of the maxillary antrum or orbital extension (IIb), or extension beyond the pterygomaxillary fossa into the infratemporal fossa (IIc). Stage III: Intracranial extension (IIIa). The tumor originates from the pterygopalatine fossa and is primarily supplied by branches of the external carotid artery. It accounts for approximately 0.05% of all head and neck tumors and is more commonly observed in children and adolescents, particularly males, with a male-to-female ratio of approximately 4:1. There is no racial predilection. Risk factors for the development of nasopharyngeal angiofibroma include the presence of a tumor in the pterygoid fossa, young age, and vascular feeders from the internal carotid artery. Early clinical features include epistaxis, facial pain, and headache, with unilateral nasal obstruction being the most common symptom. The pathogenesis of nasopharyngeal angiofibroma involves its vascular neoplasm nature, originating from the pterygopalatine fossa, and its association with the external carotid artery. Genetic alterations implicated in its development include overexpression of PDGF-B, bFGF, and Her-2/neu oncogene, as well as deletion of chromosome 17 and mutations in the tumor suppressor gene p53. Gross pathology reveals an unencapsulated, polypoid fibrous mass that bleeds upon manipulation. Microscopic findings include fibroblastic cells with plump nuclei, fibrous stroma, and abundant capillaries. The prevalence of nasopharyngeal angiofibroma is approximately 1 per 100,000 individuals worldwide. It is most commonly observed in patients aged 7–19 years. There are no known causes of the tumor. The natural history of untreated nasopharyngeal angiofibroma may lead to malignant transformation. Common complications include transient blindness, optic nerve damage, and low-grade consumption coagulopathy. Prognosis is generally favorable, with a 5-year survival rate of approximately 90% for early-stage disease and 40% for late-stage disease. Diagnosis is based on clinical criteria, including a young patient presenting with epistaxis, a smooth submucosal mass in the posterior nasal cavity, and imaging findings. Imaging modalities such as CT and MRI are essential for diagnosis. CT findings include bony changes, a non-encapsulated soft tissue mass, and anterior bowing of the posterior wall of the maxillary antrum. MRI findings include intermediate signal intensity on T1-weighted images, heterogeneous signal on T2-weighted images with flow voids, and prominent enhancement on T1 post-contrast images. Nasal endoscopy may also aid in diagnosis. Treatment primarily involves surgery, which is the mainstay of therapy. The surgical approach depends on the stage of the tumor. For early-stage disease, intranasal endoscopic surgery is the treatment of choice. For late-stage disease, approaches such as the infratemporal fossa approach or mid-facial degloving are preferred. Preoperative medical therapy, including hormonal therapy (e.g., flutamide) or radiotherapy (e.g., stereotactic radiotherapy), may be used to reduce blood loss during surgery. There are no primary preventive measures for nasopharyngeal angiofibroma. After successful treatment, patients are followed up postoperatively at intervals of 3, 6, or 12 months to monitor for recurrence.
